sophie, pleurant et joignant les mains: Sophie, crying and clasping her hands
Sophie, a chorar e de mãos postas

en: Sophie was scatterbrained; she often did bad things without thinking.
Here is what happened to her one day:
Her mother had some tiny fish no longer than a pin and no thicker than the quill of a pigeon feather.
Madame de Réan was very fond of her little fish, which lived in a basin full of water with sand at the bottom, so that they could burrow into it and hide.
Every morning Madame de Réan brought bread to her little fish; Sophie liked watching them as they pounced on the breadcrumbs and squabbled over them.
One day her father gave her a pretty little tortoiseshell knife; Sophie, delighted with her knife, used it to cut her bread, her apples, biscuits, flowers and so on.
One morning Sophie was playing; her nanny had given her some bread, which she had cut into little pieces, some almonds, which she was cutting into slices, and some lettuce leaves;
she asked her nanny for oil and vinegar to make the salad.
"No," answered the nanny; "I'll gladly give you salt, but no oil or vinegar, which could stain your dress."
Sophie took the salt and put some on her salad; she had a lot left over.
"What if I had something to salt?" she said to herself.
I don't want to salt bread; I'd need meat or fish…
Oh, what a good idea!
I'll salt Mama's little fish; I'll cut some of them into slices with my knife and salt the others whole; what fun it will be!
What a pretty dish it will make!"

And off goes Sophie without stopping to think that her mother will no longer have the pretty little fish she loves so much, and that the poor little things will suffer terribly from being salted alive or cut into slices.

Sophie runs into the drawing room where the little fish were; she goes up to the basin, fishes them all out, puts them on a plate from her toy dinner set, goes back to her little table, takes a few of the poor little fish and lays them out on a dish.
But the fish, which didn't feel comfortable out of the water, wriggled and jumped as much as they could.
To make them keep still, Sophie pours salt on their backs, their heads and their tails.
And indeed they stop moving: the poor little things were dead.
When her plate was full, she took some others and began cutting them into slices.
At the first stroke of the knife the unfortunate fish twisted desperately; but they soon stopped moving, because they were dying.

After the second fish, Sophie realised that she was killing them by cutting them into pieces; she looked anxiously at the salted fish; seeing that they weren't moving, she examined them carefully and saw that they were all dead.
Sophie went as red as a cherry.
"What will Mama say?" she said to herself.
What will become of me, poor wretched me!
How can I hide this?"
She thought for a moment.
Her face brightened; she had found an excellent way to make sure her mother wouldn't notice anything.
She quickly gathered up all the salted and sliced fish, put them back on a little plate, slipped quietly out of the room and took them back to their basin.
"Mama will think," she said, "that they fought, that they tore each other to pieces and killed each other.
I'll wipe my plates and my knife and put away my salt; luckily nanny didn't notice that I went to get the fish; she's busy with her sewing and isn't thinking about me."
Sophie went back into her room without a sound, sat down again at her little table and went on playing with her dinner set.
After a while she got up, took a book and began looking at the pictures.
But she was uneasy; she wasn't paying attention to the pictures; she kept thinking she could hear her mother coming.
All of a sudden Sophie jumps and blushes; she hears the voice of Madame de Réan calling the servants;
she hears her speaking loudly, as if she were scolding; the servants come and go;
Madame de Réan was calling the servants.
Sophie is terrified that her mother will call her nanny, or call her; but everything calms down and she hears nothing more.
The nanny, who had also heard the noise and was curious, put down her sewing and went out.
She comes back a quarter of an hour later.
"How lucky," she says to Sophie, "that we both stayed in our room without going out!
Just imagine, your mother has just been to see her fish; she found them all dead, some whole, others cut into pieces.
She called all the servants together to ask them which wicked person had killed those poor little creatures; nobody could or would say anything.
I've just met her; she asked me whether you had been in the drawing room;
luckily I was able to tell her that you hadn't moved from here, that you'd been having fun playing at dinner parties with your little dinner set.
'It's strange,' she said, 'I'd have bet it was Sophie who did this fine deed.'
'Oh, madam,' I answered her, 'Sophie isn't capable of doing something so wicked.'
'So much the better,' said your mother, 'because I would have punished her severely.
It's lucky for her that you didn't leave her and that you can assure me she can't have killed my poor fish.'
'Oh, as for that, madam, I'm quite sure of it,' I answered."
Sophie said nothing; she stayed still and red, her head bowed, her eyes full of tears.
For a moment she felt like confessing to her nanny that she was the one who had done it all, but her courage failed her.
The nanny, seeing her sad, thought it was the death of the poor little fish that was upsetting her.
"I was quite sure," she said, "that you'd be as sad as your mother about what happened to those poor little creatures.
But you must tell yourself that those fish weren't happy in their prison: because that basin really was a prison for them; now that they're dead, they're not suffering any more.
So don't think about it any more, and come here so I can get you ready to go to the drawing room; dinner will be served soon."
Sophie let herself be combed and washed without a word; she went into the drawing room; her mother was there.
"Sophie," she said to her, "has your nanny told you what happened to my little fish?
Yes, Mama.
If your nanny hadn't assured me that you'd stayed in your room with her since you left me, I would have thought it was you who killed them;
all the servants say it wasn't any of them.

But I think that Simon, the servant whose job it was to change the water and sand in the basin every morning, wanted to get rid of that chore, and killed my poor fish so he wouldn't have to look after them any more.
So I'll dismiss him tomorrow.
Oh, Mama, that poor man!
What will become of him, with his wife and children?
Too bad for him; he shouldn't have killed my little fish, which had never done him any harm, and which he made suffer by cutting them into pieces.
But it wasn't him, Mama!
I promise you it wasn't him!
How do you know it wasn't him? I believe it was him, that it can only have been him, and tomorrow I'll send him away.
Oh no, Mama, don't do that.
It was me who took the little fish and killed them.
You!… What nonsense!
You loved those little fish, you would never have made them suffer and die!
I can see you're saying that to excuse Simon…
No, Mama, I promise you it was me; yes, it was me; I didn't mean to kill them, I only wanted to salt them, and I thought the salt wouldn't hurt them.
I didn't think cutting them would hurt them either, because they didn't cry out.
But when I saw they were dead, I took them back to their basin, without my nanny, who was sewing, seeing me go out or come back in."
Madame de Réan was so astonished by Sophie's confession that for a few moments she didn't answer.
Sophie timidly raised her eyes and saw her mother's eyes fixed on her, but without anger or sternness.

"Sophie," Madame de Réan said at last, "if I had found out what you've just told me by chance, that is, by the will of God, who always punishes the wicked, I would have punished you mercilessly and severely.
But the good feeling that made you confess your fault to clear Simon will earn you forgiveness.

So I won't scold you, because I'm quite sure you feel how cruel you were to those poor little fish by not thinking, first, that the salt was bound to kill them, and second, that it's impossible to cut up and kill any creature without it suffering."
And, seeing that Sophie was crying, she added:
"Don't cry, Sophie, and don't forget that confessing your faults is how you get them forgiven."
Sophie wiped her eyes and thanked her mother, but she stayed a little sad all day for having caused the death of her little friends the fish.
pt: A Sophie era distraída; fazia muitas vezes asneiras sem pensar.
Eis o que lhe aconteceu um dia:
A mãe tinha uns peixinhos não maiores do que um alfinete e não mais grossos do que o cano de uma pena de pombo.
A senhora de Réan gostava muito dos seus peixinhos, que viviam numa bacia cheia de água com areia no fundo, para se poderem enterrar e esconder.
Todas as manhãs a senhora de Réan levava pão aos peixinhos; a Sophie divertia-se a vê-los atirarem-se às migalhas e a disputá-las.
Um dia o pai deu-lhe um lindo canivete de tartaruga; a Sophie, encantada com o canivete, usava-o para cortar o pão, as maçãs, os biscoitos, as flores, etc.
Uma manhã, a Sophie estava a brincar; a ama tinha-lhe dado pão, que ela cortara em bocadinhos, amêndoas, que cortava às fatias, e folhas de alface;
pediu à ama azeite e vinagre para temperar a salada.
— Não — respondeu a ama —; dou-lhe sal de boa vontade, mas não azeite nem vinagre, que lhe podiam manchar o vestido.
A Sophie pegou no sal e pôs na salada; sobrou-lhe muito.
— E se eu tivesse alguma coisa para salgar? — disse para consigo.
Não quero salgar pão; precisava de carne ou de peixe…
Oh, que boa ideia!
Vou salgar os peixinhos da mamã; corto alguns às fatias com o meu canivete e salgo os outros inteiros; vai ser tão divertido!
Que prato tão bonito vai ficar!
E lá vai a Sophie sem pensar que a mãe vai deixar de ter os lindos peixinhos de que tanto gosta, e que os pobrezinhos vão sofrer muito por serem salgados vivos ou cortados às fatias.

A Sophie corre à sala onde estavam os peixinhos; aproxima-se da bacia, pesca-os todos, põe-nos num prato do seu serviço de brincar, volta para a mesinha, pega em alguns daqueles pobres peixinhos e estende-os numa travessa.
Mas os peixes, que não se sentiam à vontade fora de água, mexiam-se e saltavam quanto podiam.
Para os fazer ficar quietos, a Sophie deita-lhes sal nas costas, na cabeça e na cauda.
E, de facto, ficam imóveis: os pobrezinhos estavam mortos.
Quando o prato ficou cheio, pegou noutros e começou a cortá-los às fatias.
Ao primeiro golpe de canivete, os infelizes peixes contorciam-se desesperados; mas ficavam logo imóveis, porque morriam.

Depois do segundo peixe, a Sophie percebeu que os matava ao cortá-los aos bocados; olhou preocupada para os peixes salgados; vendo que não se mexiam, examinou-os com atenção e viu que estavam todos mortos.
A Sophie ficou vermelha como uma cereja.
— Que vai dizer a mamã? — disse para consigo.
Que vai ser de mim, pobre desgraçada!
Como é que hei de esconder isto?
Pensou um momento.
O rosto iluminou-se-lhe; tinha encontrado uma maneira excelente de a mãe não dar por nada.
Apanhou depressa todos os peixes salgados e cortados, voltou a pô-los num pratinho, saiu devagarinho do quarto e levou-os de volta para a bacia.
— A mamã vai pensar — disse ela — que eles se bateram, que se despedaçaram e se mataram uns aos outros.
Vou limpar os pratos e o canivete e arrumar o sal; felizmente a ama não reparou que fui buscar os peixes; está ocupada com a costura e não pensa em mim.
A Sophie voltou sem barulho para o quarto, sentou-se outra vez à mesinha e continuou a brincar com o serviço.
Passado algum tempo, levantou-se, pegou num livro e pôs-se a ver as imagens.
Mas estava inquieta; não prestava atenção às imagens; parecia-lhe sempre ouvir a mãe a chegar.
De repente, a Sophie estremece e cora; ouve a voz da senhora de Réan, que chamava os criados;
ouve-a falar alto, como se estivesse a ralhar; os criados vão e vêm;
A senhora de Réan chamava os criados.
A Sophie treme com medo de que a mãe chame a ama, ou que a chame a ela; mas tudo se acalma e deixa de ouvir alguma coisa.
A ama, que também tinha ouvido barulho e era curiosa, deixa a costura e sai.
Volta um quarto de hora depois.
— Que sorte — diz ela à Sophie — termos estado as duas no quarto sem sair!
Imagine que a sua mãe acabou de ir ver os peixes; encontrou-os todos mortos, uns inteiros, outros cortados aos bocados.
Mandou vir todos os criados para lhes perguntar quem era o malvado que tinha matado aqueles pobres bichinhos; ninguém pôde ou quis dizer nada.
Acabei de a encontrar; perguntou-me se a menina tinha estado na sala;
felizmente pude responder-lhe que a menina não tinha saído daqui, que se tinha divertido a brincar aos jantares com o seu servicinho.
«É estranho», disse ela, «era capaz de apostar que foi a Sophie que fez esta proeza.»
«Oh, minha senhora», respondi-lhe, «a Sophie não é capaz de fazer uma coisa tão má.»
«Ainda bem», disse a sua mãe, «porque eu tê-la-ia castigado severamente.
Sorte a dela a senhora não a ter deixado e poder garantir-me que ela não pode ter matado os meus pobres peixes.»
«Oh, quanto a isso, minha senhora, tenho toda a certeza», respondi.
A Sophie não dizia nada; estava imóvel e vermelha, de cabeça baixa e olhos cheios de lágrimas.
Por um instante teve vontade de confessar à ama que tinha sido ela a fazer tudo, mas faltou-lhe a coragem.
A ama, vendo-a triste, julgou que era a morte dos pobres peixinhos que a afligia.
— Eu tinha a certeza — disse ela — de que ia ficar triste como a sua mãe com a desgraça que aconteceu àqueles pobres bichinhos.
Mas tem de pensar que aqueles peixes não eram felizes na prisão deles: porque, no fundo, aquela bacia era uma prisão para eles; agora que estão mortos, já não sofrem.
Por isso não pense mais nisso e venha cá para eu a arranjar para ir para a sala; vai haver jantar daqui a pouco.
A Sophie deixou-se pentear e lavar sem dizer palavra; entrou na sala; a mãe estava lá.
— Sophie — disse-lhe ela —, a tua ama contou-te o que aconteceu aos meus peixinhos?
Sim, mamã.
Se a tua ama não me tivesse garantido que ficaste com ela no quarto desde que me deixaste, tinha pensado que foste tu que os mataste;
todos os criados dizem que não foi nenhum deles.
Mas acho que o criado Simon, que tinha a tarefa de mudar todas as manhãs a água e a areia da bacia, quis livrar-se dessa maçada e matou os meus pobres peixes para não ter mais de tratar deles.
Por isso vou despedi-lo amanhã.
Oh, mamã, aquele pobre homem!
Que vai ser dele, com a mulher e os filhos?
Pior para ele; não devia ter matado os meus peixinhos, que não lhe tinham feito mal nenhum, e que fez sofrer ao cortá-los aos bocados.
Mas não foi ele, mamã!
Juro-lhe que não foi ele!
Como é que sabes que não foi ele? Eu acho que foi ele, que só pode ter sido ele, e amanhã mesmo mando-o embora.
Oh, não, mamã, não faça isso.
Fui eu que tirei os peixinhos e os matei.
Tu!… Que disparate!
Tu, que gostavas tanto daqueles peixinhos, não os terias feito sofrer e morrer!
Bem vejo que dizes isso para desculpar o Simon…
Não, mamã, juro-lhe que fui eu; sim, fui eu; não os queria matar, só os queria salgar, e julgava que o sal não lhes fazia mal.
Também não julgava que cortá-los lhes fizesse mal, porque eles não gritavam.
Mas, quando os vi mortos, levei-os de volta para a bacia, sem que a ama, que estava a trabalhar, me visse sair nem entrar.
A senhora de Réan ficou tão espantada com a confissão da Sophie que durante uns instantes não respondeu.
A Sophie levantou timidamente os olhos e viu os da mãe fixos nela, mas sem raiva nem severidade.

— Sophie — disse por fim a senhora de Réan —, se eu tivesse sabido por acaso, isto é, pela vontade de Deus, que castiga sempre os maus, o que me acabaste de contar, ter-te-ia castigado sem piedade e com severidade.
Mas o bom sentimento que te fez confessar a tua falta para desculpar o Simon vai valer-te o perdão.

Por isso não te vou repreender, porque tenho a certeza de que sentes como foste cruel com aqueles pobres peixinhos por não pensares, primeiro, que o sal os ia matar e, depois, que é impossível cortar e matar um bicho qualquer sem que ele sofra.
E, vendo que a Sophie chorava, acrescentou:
— Não chores, Sophie, e não te esqueças de que confessar as tuas faltas é a maneira de seres perdoada.
A Sophie limpou os olhos e agradeceu à mãe, mas ficou o dia todo um bocadinho triste por ter causado a morte dos seus amiguinhos, os peixes.
